Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: Not a conventional food in the Indian diet - requires extensive processing to remove bitter, digestion-irritating tannins before it is safe to eat
How Much to Eat Per Day: Not recommended for children unless properly and repeatedly leached by an experienced adult; not a routine snack food

Name of the Entity: Betel Nut / Areca Nut (Supari - Areca catechu)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Contains Arecoline (an addictive stimulant alkaloid) and tannins; classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) as a Group 1 human carcinogen, strongly linked to oral cancer and oral submucous fibrosis
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: NOT a food with health benefits for children. Regular chewing/consumption carries serious cancer and addiction risk. This item should not appear on a children's 'good foods to eat' dashboard
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do NOT recommend any daily amount for children - areca nut consumption should be actively discouraged, not portioned

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Raw shea nuts contain saponins and are not conventionally eaten directly; primarily processed (pressed) into shea butter, a fat used in cosmetics and, in some West African cuisines, cooking
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: Not a direct snack/food item for children - relevant mainly as a source of shea butter (a fat), not as a nut to be eaten
How Much to Eat Per Day: Not recommended for direct consumption; not a conventional food item in the Indian diet

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Approx. 655 kcal (roasted), Healthy Fat ~60g, Protein ~24g (high); good source of Magnesium and Iron. Raw seeds contain a natural toxin and must always be roasted before eating
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: Once properly roasted, a high-protein, high-iron traditional African nut that can support growth and blood health; must never be eaten raw
How Much to Eat Per Day: Not conventionally available in India; if consumed, only in small amounts (~15g), always fully roasted

Name of the Entity: Cedar Nut / Siberian Pine Nut (Pinus sibirica)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): ~669 kcal, Healthy Fat ~68g, Protein ~14g (notably rich in the amino acid Arginine); good source of Vitamin E, Manganese and Zinc
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: Arginine content supports growth-hormone-related processes during the teen growth phase; healthy fats support brain development; zinc supports immunity
How Much to Eat Per Day: 1 small handful (~10-15g), occasionally

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Approx. 240-300 kcal (much lower fat than typical nuts, more starchy like a chestnut), Protein ~6-9g, Fat ~1-3g; must be cooked (boiled/roasted) before eating
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: A low-fat, starchy traditional food providing steady carbohydrate energy once cooked; not conventionally available in India but nutritionally similar to chestnuts
How Much to Eat Per Day: Not conventionally available in India; if consumed, only after thorough cooking, similar portion to chestnuts (~30-40g)

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Contains Benzyl isothiocyanate and Carpaine; nutrition data is not well standardized as it is not a conventional food; used occasionally, in very small quantities, as a black-pepper substitute
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: Not established as a health food for children - some research raises concerns about effects at higher intakes, and there is no established safe daily amount for this age group
How Much to Eat Per Day: Not recommended as a regular food for children; at most, an occasional, very small culinary garnish (a few seeds), not a snack

Nutritious Components (per 100g): ~316 kcal, Fat ~2g (low), Protein ~3g, Carbs ~65g, Fiber ~14g; good source of Vitamin C and antioxidants; used as a sour spice, not a snack
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: Adds tangy flavour and antioxidants to chaats and curries without needing extra salt; Vitamin C supports immunity; used in small amounts as a spice rather than eaten in quantity
How Much to Eat Per Day: 1/2 to 1 teaspoon (~2-3g) used in cooking/chaats, not eaten as a standalone snack

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Not conventionally eaten directly - raw seeds are hard, bitter and tannic; primarily processed into grape seed oil or extract, which is rich in Vitamin E and linoleic acid
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: Not a direct snack food for children; if used at all, it is as a small amount of cooking oil (grapeseed oil) rather than as eaten seeds
How Much to Eat Per Day: Not recommended for direct consumption; whole grape seeds are usually discarded when eating grapes

Name of the Entity: Apricot Kernel (Khumani Beej / Chulu - Prunus armeniaca)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Contains Amygdalin, a cyanogenic compound that releases cyanide when metabolized; bitter apricot kernels are particularly high-risk. Food safety bodies (including EFSA) advise strict limits, with children advised against eating them at all
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: NOT recommended for children. There is documented risk of cyanide poisoning from eating apricot kernels, especially in children, who are more vulnerable due to lower body weight
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do NOT include in a children's diet - no safe daily portion should be suggested for this age group

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Like other stone-fruit kernels, contains cyanogenic compounds (amygdalin-related); not conventionally eaten and not established as a safe food
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: NOT recommended for children - carries a similar cyanide-release risk to apricot and peach kernels, with no established safe consumption level for this age group
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do NOT include in a children's diet - discard when eating the plum fruit

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Contains Amygdalin (a cyanogenic glycoside); used in very small, specially processed doses in some traditional medicine systems for adults, but not a food item
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: NOT recommended for children as a food - raw peach kernels carry a cyanide-release risk; any traditional medicinal use is for adults under professional guidance only, not as a snack
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do NOT include in a children's diet - discard when eating the peach fruit

Name of the Entity: Cherry Pit Kernel / Mahleb (Prunus avium / Prunus mahaleb)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): The mahleb spice (from specially processed St. Lucie cherry kernels, Prunus mahaleb) is used in tiny pinch-sized amounts in Middle Eastern/Mediterranean baking; raw cherry pits from ordinary eating cherries contain cyanogenic compounds and should never be cracked and eaten
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: As the processed mahleb spice, adds a mild almond-like flavour to baked goods in trace amounts; ordinary cherry pits are not a food item and should always be discarded, never cracked open and eaten by children
How Much to Eat Per Day: Only as a trace pinch of mahleb spice in baked recipes; never let children eat cracked-open cherry pits directly

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Contains Persin, a compound that can cause gastrointestinal irritation; the avocado seed is not a recognised food item and has no established nutrient composition for human consumption
Benefits of Eating (for 11-15 yr student: NOT recommended for consumption. Health authorities generally advise against eating avocado seeds due to persin content and lack of safety data, especially for children
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do NOT include in a children's diet - discard when eating the avocado fruit

Name of the Entity: Date Seed (Roasted/Coffee alternative) (Khajoor Guthli - Phoenix dactylifera)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Roasted, ground date pits brewed like coffee grounds; not chewed/eaten as a nut. Per 100g of ground roasted seed: ~7 kcal negligible when brewed as a drink (most nutrients stay in the grounds); rich in dietary fibre and polyphenols; naturally caffeine-free.
How Much to Eat Per Day: As an occasional beverage only (1 small cup), not as a food portion — it is brewed and the grounds are usually discarded.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): 619 kcal, Protein 24.1g, Fat 59.3g (mostly poly-unsaturated omega-3/6), Carbs 9.6g, Fibre 6.8g. Good source of manganese, copper and magnesium. (Source: USDA FoodData Central)
How Much to Eat Per Day: 4-5 kernel halves (about 15g) a few times a week.

Name of the Entity: White Walnut / Butternut (Safed Akhrot - Juglans cinerea)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): ~612 kcal, Protein ~23.7g, Fat ~61.2g, Carbs ~3.4g, Fibre ~6g. Rich in vitamin E and omega-3 ALA, similar profile to black walnut. (USDA reference values; a less-studied nut than common walnut)
How Much to Eat Per Day: 3-4 kernel halves (about 12-15g) a few times a week.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Closely related botanically to the common walnut; approximate values (no dedicated large nutrition database exists for this variety): ~650 kcal, Protein ~15g, Fat ~65g, Carbs ~14g per 100g, mainly unsaturated fat.
How Much to Eat Per Day: 4-5 kernels (about 15g) a few times a week.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): 657 kcal, Protein 12.7g, Fat 64.4g, Carbs 12.8g, Fibre 6.4g. High in manganese, thiamin and potassium. (Source: USDA FoodData Central)
How Much to Eat Per Day: 3-4 kernels (about 12-15g) a few times a week.

Name of the Entity: Cobnut (Wild Hazelnut - Corylus avellana var. grandis)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): 628 kcal, Protein 15g, Fat 61g, Carbs 17g, Fibre 9.7g. Excellent source of vitamin E and manganese. (Hazelnut-family USDA values; cobnut is a large-fruited hazelnut cultivar)
How Much to Eat Per Day: 8-10 kernels (about 15-20g) a few times a week.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): 628 kcal, Protein 15g, Fat 61g, Carbs 17g, Fibre 9.7g — nutritionally identical to hazelnut (filbert is simply the larger-fruited hazelnut species). (USDA hazelnut values)
How Much to Eat Per Day: 8-10 kernels (about 15-20g) a few times a week.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Note: this is a starchy aquatic corm/tuber, not a true nut or seed. 97 kcal, Protein 1.4g, Fat 0.2g, Carbs 23.9g, Fibre 3g, Potassium 584mg. (Source: USDA FoodData Central)
How Much to Eat Per Day: 4-5 whole pieces (about 50g) as an occasional snack.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Approximate values for dried, ground seed (regional food-composition studies, not a standard USDA entry): ~360 kcal, Protein ~9g, Fat ~1.6g, Carbs ~78g, Fibre ~很high (~30g+), good calcium and tryptophan content.
How Much to Eat Per Day: 1-2 tbsp of roasted/ground seed (as flour/porridge, common preparation) occasionally.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Approx. per 100g (Brazil-nut relative): Fat 48-61g, Protein 16-20g, Fibre 16-23g. EXTREMELY high selenium (documented at 26,000-47,000 micrograms per kg, i.e. very many times a teen's full-day selenium requirement of ~55mcg). Two published poisoning cases of acute selenium toxicity from eating these nuts exist in the literature.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Not recommended for regular consumption by students; if eaten at all, no more than 1 small kernel, very occasionally.

Name of the Entity: Malabar Chestnut (Pachira Nut / Saba Nut - Pachira aquatica)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Limited standardized nutrition database; roasted seeds taste like peanut/chestnut. Approximate: ~370 kcal, Protein ~8g, Fat ~3-5g, Carbs high (mostly starch), moderate fibre.
How Much to Eat Per Day: A small roasted handful (15-20g) occasionally.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Not applicable — this is not a food item. The nut's sap/shell contains a caustic phenolic resin (bhilawanol) that causes severe skin blistering and burns on contact.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do not include in a student snack list. Not for consumption.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Not applicable — this is not a food item. Contains saponins (toxic if ingested; hemolytic).
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do not include in a student snack list. Not for consumption.

Name of the Entity: Palmyra Palm Nut (Taal / Munjal Kernel - Borassus flabellifer)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Limited standardized database. The soft immature jelly-seed (tadgola) is watery and low-calorie (~40-90 kcal/100g, high water content); the hard mature 'munjal' kernel is fibre-rich and starchy. Values vary a lot by ripeness stage.
How Much to Eat Per Day: 1-2 pieces of the young jelly seed (tadgola) as a seasonal, hot-weather snack.

Name of the Entity: Indian Beech Seed (Pongamia Seed - Pongamia pinnata)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Not applicable — this is not a food item. Seed oil is described in scientific literature as inedible; seeds contain the toxic flavonoid karanjin and are used for biodiesel, lamp oil and soap.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do not include in a student snack list. Not for consumption.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Kernel is ~41-42% fat, ~17% protein; the extracted fat ('kokum butter') is edible and used like ghee in Konkan cooking. Not typically eaten as a raw kernel/snack.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Consumed only as a small amount of cooking fat (1 tsp kokum butter), not as a snack kernel.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Not an established food item — Champa (Magnolia champaca) is grown for its fragrant flowers (used in perfumery/temple offerings); the seed has no documented standard human-food use or nutrition profile.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do not include in a student snack list.

Name of the Entity: Kapok Seed (Safed Simal Beej - Ceiba pentandra)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Not typically eaten directly. Seed oil (after processing) is used in some regions for cooking/soap; raw seeds are reported to contain cyclopropenoid fatty acids (a compound family also flagged in raw cottonseed) that need processing to remove.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do not include in a student snack list as a raw seed.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Not applicable — this is not a food item. Contains simmondsin-type compounds that are toxic to humans; the wax/oil is for cosmetic use only.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do not include in a student snack list. Not for consumption.

Name of the Entity: Cleome Seeds (Jakhiya / Wild Mustard - Cleome viscosa)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Used only as a tempering/seasoning spice (Uttarakhand cuisine), not eaten in nut-like quantities. Approx per 100g of seed: energy-dense, oil content moderate; no large-scale nutrition database exists — treat this as a spice, not a snack food.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Only as a cooking spice (a pinch, less than 1g per dish), never as a snack portion.

Name of the Entity: Brown Mustard Seeds (Bhuri Sarson - Brassica juncea)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): 508 kcal, Protein 26.1g, Fat 36.2g, Carbs 28.1g, Fibre 12.2g. Rich in selenium and omega-3 ALA. (Source: USDA FoodData Central) — used as a spice, not eaten in nut-sized portions.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Used only as a cooking spice (a few grams per dish, i.e. a pinch to 1 tsp), not as a snack.

Name of the Entity: Black Cumin (Kala Jeera / Bunium - Bunium persicum)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Approx. (spice-seed family): ~375 kcal, Protein ~18g, Fat ~22g, Carbs ~44g, Fibre ~11g, high iron. Used as a flavouring spice, not a snack.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Used only as a cooking spice (less than 1g per dish), not as a snack.

Name of the Entity: Bitter Fennel Seeds (Kadu Saunf - Foeniculum vulgare var. vulgare)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): 345 kcal, Protein 15.8g, Fat 14.9g, Carbs 52.3g, Fibre 39.8g, Calcium 1196mg, Iron 18.5mg per 100g. (Source: USDA FoodData Central) — eaten in small spice/mouth-freshener quantities.
How Much to Eat Per Day: 1/2 to 1 teaspoon (about 2-3g) after meals.

Name of the Entity: Sweet Fennel Seeds (Mithi Saunf - Foeniculum vulgare var. dulce)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Same USDA fennel-seed profile: 345 kcal, Protein 15.8g, Fat 14.9g, Carbs 52.3g, Fibre 39.8g, Calcium 1196mg, Iron 18.5mg per 100g.
How Much to Eat Per Day: 1/2 to 1 teaspoon (about 2-3g) after meals.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Approx per 100g: ~454 kcal, Protein ~24g, Fat ~24g, rich in iron and folate. Eaten in small quantities (soaked in milk or mixed into laddoos), not as a bulk snack.
How Much to Eat Per Day: 1 teaspoon (about 3-5g), soaked, a few times a week — not more, as excess can be strongly heating/laxative.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Alfalfa is almost always eaten as sprouts rather than dry seed; sprouts are very low-calorie (~23 kcal/100g, Protein 4g, Fibre 1.9g). Reliable nutrition data for the dry seed itself is limited.
How Much to Eat Per Day: A small handful of sprouts (20-30g) added to a meal, occasionally.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Approx (ajwain-family spice seed): ~392 kcal, Protein ~18g, Fat ~25g, Fibre ~11g. Used as a strong-flavoured spice, not a snack.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Used only as a cooking spice (under 1g per dish), not as a snack.

Name of the Entity: Bishop's Weed Seeds (Chhoti Ajwain - Ammi majus)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Not a standard food seed. Ammi majus contains furocoumarins (used medicinally for skin conditions) that can cause photosensitivity (skin reacting badly to sunlight) if consumed in meaningful amounts.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do not include in a student snack list.

Name of the Entity: Wild Celery Seeds (Banya Ajmod - Angelica glauca)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): This Himalayan plant ('Chora'/Indian angelica) is used mainly for its aromatic root as a spice; standardized nutrition data for the seed specifically is not established.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Used only as a cooking spice in small pinches, not as a snack.

Name of the Entity: Grains of Paradise (Alligator Pepper - Aframomum melegueta)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): A peppery West African spice seed; no major standardized nutrition database entry exists. Used like black pepper, in pinches.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Used only as a cooking spice (a pinch), not as a snack.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): 311 kcal, Protein 10.8g, Fat 6.7g, Carbs 68.5g, Fibre 28g, very high manganese. (Source: USDA FoodData Central) — used as a spice.
How Much to Eat Per Day: 1-2 pods (a pinch of seeds) in food or milk, not eaten by the spoonful.

Name of the Entity: Black Cardamom Seeds (Badi Elaichi Beej - Amomum subulatum)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Similar spice-seed profile to green cardamom (approx. Protein ~10g, Fat ~7g, Fibre high) though a distinct, smokier-flavoured species; used as a savoury spice, not a sweet one.
How Much to Eat Per Day: 1 pod (a pinch of seeds) per dish, not eaten by the spoonful.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Used almost entirely as a natural food colouring (bixin pigment) infused into oil — the hard seeds themselves are not chewed and eaten. No standard 'per-100g eaten' nutrition profile applies.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Used only as a colouring agent (a few seeds infused in oil), not eaten directly.

Name of the Entity: Bottle Gourd Seeds (Lauki Beej - Lagenaria siceraria)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Not a commercially eaten seed in India — usually discarded when cooking the vegetable. No standardized nutrition database entry exists for this specific seed.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Not typically eaten; no standard portion exists.

Name of the Entity: Bitter Gourd Seeds (Karela Beej - Momordica charantia)

Name of the Entity: Winter Melon Seeds (Safed Petha Beej - Benincasa hispida)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Occasionally dried and used in traditional medicine preparations; approximate cucurbit-seed range (fat ~40-45g, protein ~25-30g per 100g) based on related gourd seeds, but no dedicated large nutrition database exists for this specific seed.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Not a standard snack food; if used at all, only in very small amounts.

Name of the Entity: Zucchini Seeds (Courgette Seeds - Cucurbita pepo var.)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Same species as pumpkin, so nutritionally similar to pumpkin seeds when mature and roasted: approx. 559 kcal, Protein 30g, Fat 49g, Carbs 11g, Fibre 6g, rich in zinc and magnesium. Name of the Entity: Butternut Squash Seeds (Squash Beej - Cucurbita moschata)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Same genus as pumpkin; approximate pumpkin-seed-like profile: ~559 kcal, Protein ~30g, Fat ~49g, Fibre ~6g, rich in magnesium and zinc. (Approximate, based on the closely related pumpkin-seed reference)
How Much to Eat Per Day: A small roasted handful (15-20g) a few times a week.

Name of the Entity: Chayote Seed (Chow Chow Kernel - Sechium edule)

Name of the Entity: Ogbono Seeds (Wild Mango Seed - Irvingia gabonensis)

How Much to Eat Per Day: At most 2-3 roasted seeds occasionally — not a daily snack.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Not applicable as a food. The lychee seed/unripe aril is documented to contain hypoglycin A and MCPG, compounds linked to serious acute encephalopathy outbreaks in undernourished children in litchi-growing regions of Bihar, India.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do not include in a student snack list under any circumstances.

Nutritious Components (per 100g): Not a standard food item. Raw rambutan seeds contain saponins/tannins and are reported to have narcotic/toxic effects; some regional traditions roast them thoroughly in small amounts, but this is not a recommended practice for children.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Do not include in a student snack list.

Name of the Entity: Pecan Nut (Wild) (Junglee Pecan - Carya illinoinensis sylvestris)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): 691 kcal, Protein 9.2g, Fat 72g, Carbs 13.9g, Fibre 9.6g, very high manganese. (Source: USDA FoodData Central, common pecan values — wild pecan is the same species)
How Much to Eat Per Day: 4-5 halves (about 15g) a few times a week.

Name of the Entity: Yellow Mustard Seeds (Pili Sarson - Brassica alba)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): Approx. 508 kcal, Protein ~25g, Fat ~28-36g, Carbs ~28g, Fibre ~12g, good selenium content — similar family profile to brown mustard. Used as a spice, not a snack.
How Much to Eat Per Day: Used only as a cooking spice (a pinch to 1 tsp per dish), not as a snack.

Name of the Entity: White Chia Seeds (Safed Chia - Salvia hispanica 'White')
Nutritious Components (per 100g): 486 kcal, Protein 16.5g, Fat 30.7g (very high omega-3 ALA), Carbs 42.1g, Fibre 34.4g, Calcium 631mg. Nutritionally identical to regular chia — colour is just a natural seed-coat variant. (Source: USDA FoodData Central)
How Much to Eat Per Day: 1-2 tablespoons (about 15g) a day, soaked in water/milk before eating.

Name of the Entity: Watermelon Seeds (Roasted) (Bhuna Tarbuz Magaz - Citrullus lanatus)
Nutritious Components (per 100g): 557 kcal, Protein 28.3g, Fat 47.4g, Carbs 15.3g, high magnesium, zinc and iron. (Source: USDA FoodData Central, dried/roasted kernels)
How Much to Eat Per Day: A small roasted handful (15-20g) a few times a week.

Name of the Entity: Pine Nut (Korean) (Korean Pine Nut - Pinus koraiensis)
